title: The call from Safa
hook: he climbs Safa and asks, would you believe me if I said an army was behind this hill

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn Ishaq. Your line was: quietly first. Who did you tell one good thing to, just between the two of you? Day seven hundred thirty-two.

Ya sabahah! The cry goes up from the little hill of Safa. It's the alarm call, the one people shout when raiders are coming at dawn. Men drop what they're doing and come running. Those who can't come send someone to find out what's happening. The clans of Quraysh gather at the foot of the hill and look up. Standing on top is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The quiet season is over. Today: nadhir.
screen: `A CRY FROM THE HILL.` → `THE CLANS COME RUNNING.` → `THE QUIET SEASON IS OVER.`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the scene from Ibn Abbas. When the verse came, warn thy nearest kin, he climbed Safa and called the clans by name. When they had gathered, he did not begin with a sermon. He began with a question. If I told you that horsemen in the valley were about to attack you, would you believe me? And they answered, yes, we have only ever known you to tell the truth. Then he said: I am a warner to you, before a severe punishment. Look at how he builds it. He lets the city testify to his honesty before he says a single new thing. Years of trust, from the market, from the black stone, from Khadijah's caravans, are called in with one question. And the word he uses for himself is nadhir, a warner. Not a ruler, not a fortune-teller. Someone who has seen what's coming and shouts so others can get ready, the way the alarm call itself works. It is a word the Qur'an also uses for him. The report also says that one voice in the crowd answered him with a curse. Who it was, and what came back, is tomorrow. Today hold the question. Would you believe me? It asks what kind of life makes a person believable when it matters.
screen: `HE CALLS THE CLANS BY NAME.` · `WOULD YOU BELIEVE ME?` · `YOU HAVE ONLY TOLD THE TRUTH.` · `NADHIR: A WARNER.` · then, large: `WOULD YOU BELIEVE ME?`

segments.voice: The practice: speak one truth plainly. Settle and breathe. Think of one true thing you've been softening, avoiding or wrapping in extra words: a no, an apology, a concern, a thank-you. Find the plainest way to say it. One sentence, no decorations. Say it silently to yourself until it sounds clean. If it's safe and kind to say out loud today, plan when. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to say it well. The bell holds the time.
Nadhir, a warner. The Prophet climbs Safa, asks the clans if they'd believe him, and names himself one who warns of what's coming. Today's word.
Your line: would you believe me? Today, say one true thing plainly, the kind of plain that keeps you believable. Day seven hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims retell the call from Safa as the beginning of the public message in Mecca; pilgrims on Hajj and Umrah walk between Safa and Marwah, though that rite remembers Hajar, not this day.

original.note: Arabic: a warner, one who warns of danger ahead; the word he used for himself on Safa.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man shouting from a hill.
what it means: he asked the city to vouch for his honesty, then called himself a warner.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Abbas in al-Bukhari, after 26:214; the alarm cry ya sabahah; nadhir, a recurring Qur'anic word for the Prophet.
recall: the month the Qur'an was revealed

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4770 (Ibn Abbas: Safa; 'would you believe me?'; 'I am a warner to you')

notes: Bukhari 4770 cited from memory; some narrations (e.g. 4971) include the alarm cry 'ya sabahah'. Confirm numbers and details; the dialogue is paraphrased.
'Horsemen in the valley' follows one wording; another narration speaks of an army behind the hill (the index's wording). Confirm.
'The Qur'an uses that word for him again and again' gives no count; confirm it is fair.
The trust 'from the market, from the black stone, from Khadijah's trade' recalls earlier days on this path; confirm those scripts.
howItsDone notes that the sa'y between Safa and Marwah remembers Hajar, to avoid conflating the two; confirm.
